utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Valentin Coric's Defence has organised its submissions in the following way. The first part will be addressed by Mr. Dan Ivetic, who will respond to the questions of the Chamber sent to us in preparation for the hearing. And then I'm going to address the Appeals Chamber about the legal and factual errors dealt with in our submissions. Hopefully we will have enough time to deal with all of them in our submissions. And now I give the floor to Mr. Dan Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time we would like to address your first question on the topic on the Trial Chamber's inquiry into the alleged state of occupation being in existence during the relevant time-period. I would like to note that we discussed this in detail at paragraphs 75 to 83 of our appellants brief and we stand behind those submissions in full. We would like to stress at the outset that any inquiry into occupation in this case, under this indictment, is based on error. There was never any proper notice given to the Coric Defence in the indictment that occupation was part of the allegations charged that should be defended against. No reasonable Chamber could read paragraph 232 of the indictment as notice of occupation. Similarly, in volume 1, paragraph 91 of the judgement, the claims are that the allegation of occupation was made known to and applied against Petkovic and Praljak, but what about notice to Coric? The Chamber is silent on the issue because there was not proper notice given to Coric in the indictment. Paragraphs 8 and 10 of the indictment, Petkovic and Praljak are alleged to have "exercised de jure and/or de facto command over Herceg-Bosna/HVO armed forces," but there is no mention of occupation. Where are the key words that are necessary to provide adequate notice? Although the Prosecution claims a waiver on the issue of occupation in their response at -- response brief at paragraph 69, this argument fails as to Coric, because in that same paragraph the Prosecution concedes the Coric Defence did object to the same. We objected as soon as the Prosecution revealed occupation as part of their case, which was only at the phase of the final brief and closing arguments. Waiver is thus not an available argument. Further, assuming arguendo, even if the notice requirement were to be ignored, the Trial Chamber still erred in the course of its inquiry. We would join in the arguments made by our Defence colleagues that went before us this week, arguing against both the findings of an international armed conflict and occupation. Rather than repeating the same, I will add on to what has been said. The Trial Chamber made an error of law because it did not mention invasion as an essential element of establishing a state of occupation. The crime does not cite to evidence nor conclude that the HVO as a foreign army invaded -- that territory, after that time, is said to be occupied. The HVO did not invade from Croatia. The HVO, rather than being some foreign power, was comprised of lawful, domestic inhabitants of the very areas where they were located. That the alleged borders and occupied areas were often crossed to supply the other party, i.e., the ABiH and the HVO, with weapons, ammunition, training, et cetera, was mentioned by some of our colleagues on the other Defences earlier this week. This evidence showing the integration and the close links between the HVO and the armija BiH cannot be reconciled with the alleged existence of an international armed conflict, nor occupation of areas by hostile HVO foreign forces. We submit that the Prosecution's quotation in footnote 266 of their response confirms that very fact. All authorities agree on the same definition, namely, that a territory is occupied when it is placed under the authority of a hostile army and the state to which it belongs has ceased to exercise its own authority. According to ample evidence as we have heard this week, including, among other, 4D410, and including statements by BiH authority, the HVO was an equal and constituent part of the RBiH armed forces, on par with the armija BiH. Thus, the HVO cannot be a foreign power. As established by the Constitution of the SRBiH in Article 256 and by the Law on All People's Defence in Article 63, the Croatian communities instituted Territorial Defence and civilian protection structures, in accordance unity and neighbouring municipalities as established by the BiH state. Thus, it must be stressed that not only the HVO was not on -- that the HVO was on that same territory from the beginning and did not invade, but the HVO structures were lawful structures made up of persons who had similar positions on that territory even before the war. For instance, and it is of significance that in some area, such as Posusje, Grude, Tomislavgrad, and other places, there was not any combat nor change of authority such that existing structures and local municipal organs remained the same, even though falling under the HVO. Thus, there is no hostile force nor "invasion" and the lack of any grounds for occupation, due to the fact that these HVO areas that never could be called occupied, the whole concept of occupation fails. An armed conflict can be characterised as international if a foreign state has an overall control over subordinated armed forces that do not directly belong to it. But according to the Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 137, the control exercised must comprise more than the mere provision of financial assistance or military equipment or training. No reasonable Chamber can conclude that an international armed conflict existed or that the HVO was a foreign army, or that the Republic of Croatia provided assistance only to the HVO and not the ABiH. I will not repeat the plethora of evidence which we've heard this week of the military supplies and weapons given by Croatia to both the HVO and the armija BiH, but I will stress one bit of evidence in the case that 90 per cent of the weapons and the material technical supplies of the armija BiH were provided by the Republic of Croatia and the HVO. That's at transcript page 42146. I would also stress during all times the BiH President, Mr. Izetbegovic, travelled to other countries across Croatia. We have already heard from other Defence teams this week of the Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation in February of 1992, which recognised the armija BiH and the HVO as integral parts of the same BiH armed forces. On June 29, 1993, President Izetbegovic himself declared the HVO as a constituent part of the BiH armed forces. On April 24, 1993, the presidents of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the HVO met in Zagreb to discuss a joint command between the HVO and the ABiH. Thus, Your Honours, if we were to follow the Prosecution's logic as to some sort of de facto organ or proxy due to the support that the HVO received from Croatia, under the evidence, the armija BiH would also have to be a de facto organ or proxy of Croatia under that definition; hence, with no grounds for inquiry into occupation - no application of the additional protections that would apply in the case of occupation - is necessary. Your Honours, now I would like to address your question number 4 as it relates to the hypothetical reversal of the Trial Chamber's finding on the intent of HVO forces with regard to the deaths of the civilians who had taken refuge in Enver Sljivo's house, including the impact of the scope of the common criminal plan of the joint criminal enterprise and the alleged mens rea of our client, Valentin Coric, for murder under the first category of JCE. As a preliminary matter, I believe it was our colleague Mr. Kahn who mentioned earlier in the week a case from the United Kingdom, the Jogee case, Regina versus Jogee, cited 2016, the reference is UKSC 8, wherein the Supreme Court of England and Wales - and that came out after our briefs and therefore I think it merits a further mention - but the Supreme Court of England and Wales has essentially found that the position in English law at the time of Tadic and upon which the Appeals Chamber in Tadic relied - and look to paragraph 224, footnote 287, of the Tadic appeals judgement - upon which it relied in formulating the ICTY's JCE model was wrong. Per the Supreme Court, the correct position is that the secondary party will only be guilty of the crime committed by the principal if he intended it. That intent may be conditional upon the occurrence of facts leading up to the commission of the crime. Foresight that the crime might happen is not the correct standard, but rather, it should be based on evidence of possession of the requisite intent. That's paragraphs 83 and 92 of the Regina versus Jogee case. As the Supreme Court commented, this ruling corrects: "The striking anomaly of requiring a lower mental threshold for guilt in the case of the accessory than in the case of the principal." Paragraph 84 of the Jogee case. I leave it to Your Honours if the ICTY will correct or change its jurisprudence on the current state of law on JCE to be in line with the decision of the Supreme Court of England and Wales. We will deal with Your Honours' inquiry as to JCE 3 liability later when we discuss the two documents in relation to question 4(c)(ii). I will also try not to repeat too much what other Defence colleagues have said on the issue of -- of -- of question 4, and hereby adopt by reference especially - but not only - that events in Gornji Vakuf were an isolated local incident that cannot prove any common criminal purpose in existence. If this finding that the shelling of Enver Sljivo's house as crimes of wilful killing and murder is overturned, then the Trial Chamber's findings about the existence of a clear pattern of conduct of HVO attacks will also have to be overturned. And their conclusion of murders and wilful killings in Mostar and Heliodrom in the later period, after 30th June 1993, must also be overturned if favour of the defendant. The reason for this is rather simple. The Trial Chamber relied upon its findings of murders and wilful killings such as this shelling of Enver Sljivo's house in the course of attacks as to Gornji Vakuf and Mostar as the basis for its finding of a common criminal purpose. The Trial Judgement at paragraph 65 of volume 4 based its conclusion on a common criminal purpose on an alleged "clear pattern of conduct" on the part of HVO forces. Thus, if the aforesaid shelling of Enver Sljivo's house is overturned, then the finding of wilful killings and murder in Gornji Vakuf has no evidence to support same. Thus, the entire concept of a "clear pattern of conduct" on the part of HVO forces is then called into question and nullified, especially since there are no similar findings of wilful killings and murders in relation to other municipalities except later in Mostar. It does not fit into the theory of a Prosecution JCE. No clear pattern of conduct means no common criminal purpose, which defeats JCE 1 responsibility as to the municipalities. This means that Mr. Coric cannot be said to have had any JCE 1 criminal liability. Now, if we shift our focus to events in Mostar. First of all, if there is no viable conclusion that can be drawn from the evidence that there was a "clear pattern of conduct" and if - as we've heard from other teams this week - there is no original JCE in existence as to the municipalities, then it becomes illogical that this non-existent JCE would be expanded to include Mostar, as the Trial Chamber erroneously found in volume 4, paragraph 59 of the judgement. Murder as a "clear pattern of conduct" is essential to the Trial Chamber's conclusion that there existed a common criminal plan; and without a substantial finding of murder under the evidence, then Your Honours must acquit Mr. Coric for Count 2 and Count 3. As well as especially if it is reasonable under the evidence that the alleged crimes can also be reasonably understood as the result of strictly military operations over which Coric had no role; and second, in the -- in regards to the extended period after January until late June and July, where there is essentially no military operations whatsoever. Further, if we return to Enver Sljivo's house, the Defence must point - in addition to what our colleagues have already said - that the Prosecution draws attention to smoke rising from a chimney, but the Prosecution ignores its own concession that armed defenders were within tens of metres of that same house, or the references of my colleagues to evidence demonstrating that armed offenders were even closer to the house. Thus, there was no proper analysis performed to exclude that this shell was not part of a legitimate military operation between two opposing armed forces, wherein the unfortunate deaths of civilians would be collateral casualties. Thus, the Trial Chamber committed a legal error by merely generically categorising such shells as inherently indiscriminate weapons without doing the proper analysis called for. I remind Your Honours of the Galic Appeals Chamber that established that a shelling can only be determined to be "indiscriminate" after "determining that no reasonable or possibility existed that the victims ... were unintentionally harmed by combat in their vicinity." That's paragraph 232 to 235 of the Galic appeals judgement. There are many alternative reasonable conclusions. For instance, if there are civilians in the front lines or if defending ABiH, armija BiH, forces placed their own units near civilian structures, many conclusions which qualify the deaths as unintentional and ones for which one cannot be found militarily nor criminal liable. We also draw Your Honours' attention to the fact the Prosecution is presenting a different version than that found by the Chamber. Namely, the Prosecution says that a very precise direct fire tank round was used. If the Prosecution persists in this argument - as it has this whole week - then, Your Honours, the Prosecution is itself telling you that the trial judgement is in error. They can't have it both ways. Moving to the mens rea elements for Count 2 and 3. The Defence has consistently and in detail in its appeals brief demonstrated that Coric neither received combat reports nor had any command authority over military operations, nor even over the military police when they were used in those operations, and he was not present in the zone of combat in Gornji Vakuf. In fact, we have several bits of evidence that demonstrate that during relevant time-period, Mr. Coric is in the hospital in Zagreb. P1350; transcript testimony 50967, 51082, 51087 through 8. In volume 4 paragraph 920 to 921 of the judgement, the sole basis of Coric's knowledge that crimes must have occurred in Gornji Vakuf are cited as P1635 and P3090. At issue are reports only giving statistics of combat casualties of the military police, which can be understood as legitimate combat, and then also mentioning combat and capturing of armija BiH combatants as well as reporting on the need to increase anticrime activities. Your Honours, such reports cannot form the basis for any criminal mens rea of wilful killing or murders in Gornji Vakuf on the part of Mr. Coric. Additionally, for instance, in paragraph 33 of our appeals brief, we have discussed some of the many facets of evidence that have demonstrated that Mr. Coric did not the requisite mens rea, including his conduct in the proper professional training of military police, including on the topics of international law and the humane treatment of detainees. In paragraph 34 of our appeal brief, we discuss Coric's efforts to organise courses with the International Red Cross to further train the military police to act properly. In paragraph 35 of our appeal brief, we cite to evidence that no fewer than 2.000 criminal reports were filed by the military police against Croat perpetrators of crimes, and these criminal reports were then left to be dealt with by the appropriate judicial organs. The Defence presented copies of just some of the military prosecution office registers that it was able to find from several offices. And that is 5D4288. A large number of unfinished cases were transferred by the judicial organs -- transferred to the -- to the judicial organs to be dealt with. A large of number unfinished cases were transferred after the Washington Agreements. We have 5D5027, 5D5032, 5D5024, and the testimony of witness Vidovic at transcript page 51562 through 9 telling us that. We must stress that the role of either the military or civilian police ends with the submission of criminal reports; even the trial judgement concludes that in volume 4, paragraph 881 and 2, but we will discuss that later. In this regard it should be stressed that in the Milutinovic trial judgement, President Milutinovic was found not guilty and acquitted even though he had actually reporting of crimes because he at the same time information and foresaw that appropriate law enforcement and judicial organs were handling things to prosecute the perpetrators. This is volume 3, paragraphs 132 and 143 of the Milutinovic trial judgement. This is an acquittal the Prosecution did not appeal. Coric's actions also demonstrate that he foresaw that law enforcement and police organs would work together to prevent crimes and took all steps available to him, whilst that both the military and civilian police, to have those forces legitimately function to prevent and punish criminal activity. It cannot be excluded under the evidence that Coric too believed he was part of a legitimate state operating in a legitimate police role and that crimes were investigated and punished in accord with the law. Thus, this is in fact a more reasonable conclusion than any common criminal purpose that he would be a part of. The most significant evidence as to the lack of intent to commit crimes can be seen from two of Mr. Coric's own documents issued during the same time-period. P5471, while at the military police administration; and P6837, while at the Ministry of Interior. In both, Mr. Coric is informing everyone else and, in essence, pleading with HVO military commanders that he is lacking the military police - and then later the civilian police - to properly prevent crimes and do police jobs because the manpower has been taken and resubordinated to the HVO military for combat. Coric is asking for their return so that they can more effectively prevent and police against crimes. Your Honours, under the totality of this evidence, it is inconsistent and indeed illogical for anyone to conclude that Coric had the mens rea for crimes in Counts 2 and 3, since he is espousing a desire to prevent crimes across the entire territory. Thus, there is not any evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could have properly relied upon to infer that Coric shared or had any intent for these murders or a JCE. Thus, if the findings as to the killings in Gornji Vakuf were overturned, given this plethora of other evidence of Coric's crime-fighting in other places, it would be impossible to assess to him a criminal mens rea for JCE 1. Given the foregoing evidence, he simply cannot share the intent of the possible or alleged co-perpetrators of killings. It would be improper to do so merely based on his position as an official in police and law enforcement activities. Turning now to the issue of mens rea for JCE 3 liability. As a preliminary matter it should be stressed that if this Appeals Chamber overturns the finding as to Enver Sljivo's house and the deaths in Gornji Vakuf, then it negates even more the foreseeability of additional JCE crimes for Coric. These death must have been foreseeable as crimes of an existing common criminal purpose he agreed to - look to the Sainovic appeals judgement paragraph 1557 - rather than due to legitimate military action or some other cause like random crime, random crime that he could perhaps foresee as a police official. Again, by virtue of being a police official, Coric by definition foresees crimes; but that does not mean that he intends or condones them or that he is part of a common criminal purpose, especially, especially given the aforecited evidence that he was doing his best with limited manpower to prevent crimes and thus fulfil his police role. Further, if the earlier finding that deaths in Gornji Vakuf as murders are removed, there is no possibility for Coric to have foreseen killings in Dretelj - as erroneously concluded in volume 4, paragraph 1021 of the trial judgement, which occurred at a later date - because he would have no -- he would have no prior notice to be able to foresee the same. Your Honours, I would now like to address question number 4(c)(ii) raised by Your Honours as to the significance of Exhibits P1414 and P1393 in relation to the assessment of Coric's ability to foresee murders under JCE 3. As a preliminary matter we would stress that Mr. Coric was never part of any JCE or common criminal purpose. We would also note that it is important to consider not only the substance but the time-period of the stated documents to begin with this analysis, and to look at the totality of other evidence, including the context of how these documents were used in the trial judgement. First, P1939 is a document of the Military Police Crime Department reporting on certain less serious creams, most notably not murder, committed by military police personnel against prisoners sent to Coric in his capacity at the military police administration. P1414, the other document, is Coric's immediate order - sent the very next day after he received P1393 - seeking to investigate these specific incidents of alleged crimes and to take action against the wrong-doers. In P1414, Coric undertakes all available means at his disposal and acts properly as a military police officer. He asks, among other things for a report to be submitted of events that resulted in the maltreatment and infliction of injuries in the Tomislavgrad prison. He asks for clarification of the circumstances surrounding the bodily injuries of detainees in Ljubuski prison; to find out the names of persons who participated in those events; and the names of units they belong to; and for all stolen goods to be returned; and in the case of missing items, written explanations to be submitted. P1414 thus demonstrates that Coric neither intended for these crimes to occur nor condoned the same. Rather, P1414 shows the proper and appropriate reaction of Coric when he is informed that crimes are suspected or known to have been committed by members of the military police. Indeed, the Trial Chamber treats P1414 as proof of Coric's good deeds to try and combat criminal activity, not as incriminatory of him. Volume 4 of the trial judgement, paragraph 881, footnote 1645, which we will discuss in a bit. The record in this case unfortunately does not demonstrate if there was ever any written reply back to Coric about the results of this particular investigation or if the perpetrators could be identified and, if so, how punished. We do not know what the result was of this investigation. However, we have other evidence which demonstrated that Coric had a very strict view that forbade the commission of crimes by military policemen. For instance, the record is clear that within his limited competencies, Coric sought to have the behaviour of the military police comply with the utmost professionalism. We have Exhibit P129 that Coric sent military police units in the field rules of discipline they should follow. Likewise, Coric's personal attitude was described at trial at transcript page 50953 through 50954 as a very stringent policy as to discipline of military police found to have engaged in such misconduct such that, and now I quote: "... any such perpetrators should be prosecuted and a criminal report filed ... anybody who besmirched the name of the military police on battle-grounds throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they should be thrown out of the unit." We have other evidence that when crimes were committed by military police and made known to Coric, he adhered to precisely this stringent policy stated above by a witness and dismissed the perpetrators from their duties and called for criminal reports to be forwarded to the relevant prosecutors because, in his words as expressed in Exhibit P3571: "The above-named have sullied the honour of the military police and their further presence in the unit is detrimental." In that particular instances, those dismissed and criminally reported were perpetrators who had committed rapes. Now this one that I just read, P3571, comes later in time than P1414 and thus demonstrates that we can understand P1414 -- that is to say after P1414, Coric as chief of the military police administration, within his limited authority, fought and sought to prevent crimes committed by military police members. Respectfully, the burden of proof is not on the Defence to prove the results of the investigation ordered by P1414, but in the context of this subsequent dated evidence showing uniform conduct, it can be reasonably concluded that Coric did not condone crimes. And thus we believe that P1414 is properly understood as an order for investigations by the appellant and that it shows that he took steps where he could within his limited competency to prevent or punish crimes reported to him that involved military police personnel. Returning to what we mentioned earlier, we have to emphasise that in this light and context, P1414 is used as an example of Coric's efforts at crime prevention. P1414 is mentioned in the trial judgement not only in paragraph 881, footnote 1645 in a positive rather than negative sense, but further the next paragraph of the judgement, paragraph 882, the Trial Chamber states: "In view of the above, the Chamber finds that as chief of the military police administration, Valentin Coric had the ability to participate in fighting crime within the HVO but that his power was limited to investigating the perpetrators of crimes, while the responsibility for their prosecution rested within [sic] the Military Prosecutor." Your Honours, these paragraphs are in the section of the judgement volume 4 entitled: "Valentin Coric's Powers in Fighting Crime." Thus, it must be seen that while Coric took steps against crimes known to him, he was limited by his position as to what he could do and over whom he could exercise such discipline. Relating to this, we would like to refer to P1678. It is Coric's own document dated 17 March 1993, where he is talking about subordination of units of the military police, and he is saying that they will eliminate anyone from the military police whose work is objected to by the military commander - to which they are subordinated - or SIS. It is clear that Coric not only announces a fight against any form of crime or lack of discipline in the military police, but he also states that the military police administration would follow information received by those to whom the military police units were subordinated - military commanders - and those who would have the obligation to fight crime in all HVO units without exception. Thus, to the extent that Coric could foresee that other crimes could happen, such as murders, we have to take into account that he legitimately believed the perpetrators would be processed and punished in line with his strict stance by the appropriate organs who were not under his authority nor competence. In this regard -- in this regard, it must also be taken into account that the other document, P1393 that Your Honours asked about, is not mentioned in the judgement in connection to Mr. Coric. However, P1393 is an internal military police document. So again in this instance, Coric reacts appropriately and in line with the law when he is informed through the regular chain of informing within the military police. Thus, these documents cannot be used to infer Coric's ability to foresee murders that would not be likewise punished and subjected to an appropriate legal remedy, as he did for other crimes that he heard about. Now, further, murder is not even mentioned in these two documents that Your Honours have asked about, P1393 and P1414. Only thefts, maltreatment, and beatings were mentioned. The Prosecution - in its reply brief at paragraph 73 - concedes that foreseeability of murder is based on knowledge of previous murders and not on other crimes like theft, beatings, or maltreatment. Thus, even under the Prosecution's accepted standard, P1393 and P1414 cannot be used to infer Coric's ability to foresee murders that would not likewise be punished and subjected to appropriate legal remedy. All witnesses were clear that no post-combat reports were ever sent to Coric in any form whatsoever by the military police subordinated in combat zones to the military. The evidence is that the military police administration only received statistics such as the location, general situation of the military police such as numerical strength, casualties, et cetera. You can look to 5D5110, paragraph 5 for reference to that. As to crimes that were reported and that he notice of, Coric was put on notice that the relevant authorities were investigating, arresting, and submitting criminal reports to prosecute the perpetrators. P4058 is an example of that. We would also in this case highlight 5D2113, a report from Coric to the Defence Department that outlines anticrime measures that have been implemented in Mostar with "noticeable results," namely when the military police undertook control of parts of the city to prevent looting. Similarly, we see in 5D4110 Coric taking those steps within his limited domain to contribute to law enforcement efforts in Mostar, trying to increase the effectiveness of anticrime measures, supporting training of additional crime technicians needed, and encouraging the military police to work more closely with the civilian police. He maintained a similar position when he left the military police and became civilian minister of interior. Further, based on the two documents that Your Honours have asked about, Coric could not foresee murders that came later in a different time-period, under different circumstances, especially those carried out by personnel not within his authority and beyond his limited competencies and which were not reported to him. Time and context are quite important. It should be recalled that other evidence shows that Coric did not even have competency over all the military police because of their engagement in the front lines with the HVO military. Just the other day Mr. Stringer at transcript page 422 to 423 represented to Your Honours that the majority correctly found that that other appellants had the military police subordinated to them and did not mentioned Coric; but my colleague will deal with the resubordination of the military and civilian police later today and discuss efforts again of Coric to try to get both the military and civilian police back from the front lines to engage in law enforcement activities. Thus, at all times, Coric - by virtue of his police role - foresaw crimes but also foresaw that the law enforcement organs and judicial organs would work to prevent such crimes. If necessary, personnel were returned to be allowed to serve that function. Respectfully, we are surprised by this Appeals Chamber's question as raising new issues that neither the Prosecution's appeal nor the Prosecution's respondent's brief raised, insofar as they do not cite to these documents as to Coric. The trial judgement, we submit in volume 4, paragraph 881 and 882, recognises that Coric fought crime. It used these documents -- this document, P1414, as an example of how he performs his regular police duty. JCE on the other hand, is a form of responsibility, and we submit performing duty and fighting crime cannot be an especially part of a JCE, nor can they be viewed as furtherance of a JCE. If performing the regular duty of a police officer, to foresee and react to crime becomes a key element of a JCE or proof of a later crime; and basically the only proof then, the very essence of fighting crime itself becomes criminal, which is totally opposite and absurd to the legal systems of the world. We would remind Your Honours of the Appeals Chamber holding in the Halilovic appeal, at paragraph 59 of that judgement, wherein it is stated: "For example, a police officer may be able to prevent and punish crimes under his jurisdiction, but this would not as much make him a superior (in the sense of Article 7(3) of the Statute) vis-à-vis any perpetrator within the jurisdiction." Again, this is paragraph 59. Respectfully we would ask that the same analysis be applied as to JCE in any form. Coric's role as first a military and then a civilian policeman cannot be used to impose liability against him because his official duty always had him foresee crime but also foresee the appropriate enforcement of law by relevant organs to prevent and punish such crime, like any other policeman in the world. Any other result would make it a crime to act as a policeman. And again we must stress that these two documents at issue in question 4(c)(ii) of Your Honours' questions, they're not talking about some selective crime fighting by Coric, but they're specifically talking about prevention of crimes and punishment of those committing crimes against the most vulnerable group at that time, Muslim prisoners. So for Appellant Coric to be convicted and criminally punished for performing his police duty in an honourable manner would be a bad precedent for further judiciaries. The question that arises is: If anyone undertakes efforts to prevent and punish crimes by virtue of their police role in fighting crime, is such a person to be held automatically and strictly liable and responsible for all future crimes committed by perpetrators that he neither knew of nor could stop? Will he be punished for doing something good? Any policeman has to fight crime - that is his duty - he cannot be punished for that. And unfortunately, unfortunately, no policeman in the world - not even Mr. Coric - can be 100 per cent effective and successful in preventing or punishing all crimes that are committed within their jurisdictional area nor that he can foresee might happen. Thus, in finishing this question, we would stress that under JCE 3 what is at issue is the dolo eventualis standard, which applies when the accused did not intend to bring about a specific result but was aware that the actions of a group would lead to that result and - this is the key part - willingly took that risk. Neither of these two documents in this question, nor the totality of the evidence demonstrate that Coric either intended the crimes to occur go unpunished, let alone that he willingly took such a risk. To the contrary, he did all within his limited competencies and means to fight against that risk and tried to ensure that if crimes occurred, perpetrators were investigated and punished. Your Honours, I would like to now address question 5 as to the proposed overturning of the Trial Chamber's findings that property destruction caused in Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci and Uzricje was indiscriminate, wanton, and not justified by military necessity. Again, some of my colleagues that have spoken already have addressed this topic, and we would join in most of those submissions rather than repeat everything here. I will try only to stress a few things such that in trial judgement, volume 3, paragraph 1569, the Chamber confirms that it received evidence that members of the armija BiH were present in the towns of Gornji Vakuf and, precisely, in the villages of Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci, and Uzricje at the time of the HVO attack and the alleged destruction of the houses. Some armed Muslim men were even hidden inside the houses from time to time. Yet, the Trial Chamber established that the shelling of these villages was indiscriminate. Further, the Trial Chamber explicitly found that in Uzricje, where military policemen resubordinated to the HVO military were deployed, there were also armed Muslim men. This village was thus defended by an armed opposing military force comprised of Muslim men. Look to the trial judgement volume 2, paragraph 370, and the same was true for the situation in Zdrimci and Hrasnica. These are not undefended localities. We do not have any information on the placement of the civilians, that is to say how far were the civilians from the combat zone, from the front lines, or the defenders or combatants; nor do we have any information on the quantity of the shelling; nor do we have expert or other evidence that would clearly describe all the conditions related to the shelling which would be necessary to assess the same. The burden of proof is on the Prosecution, and they did not present any evidence on that matter. So no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that there was only one conclusion available under the evidence; namely, that is indiscriminate, because there is a reasonable doubt in that conclusion. Multiple, alternative conclusions are available under the evidence, including legitimate combat. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber does not draw distinction between when military necessity ends and indiscriminate acts begin, at what moment something that had a military necessity becomes indiscriminate. This is strange, having in mind that the Trial Chamber recognised that there were armija BiH fighters on the ground and even HVO combat losses from fighting with the ABiH forces in these same villages. The other day I heard Prosecutor Stringer downplay the level of combat in this area. That was transcript page 419. But please we urge you to look at the evidentiary record that you have before you, where there were significant casualties from this combat in these villages. For instance, P3090. Here we see that just from the military police that were subordinated to the HVO military in that area in this time, they had 10 dead and 63 wounded resulting from battles. This means, at the very least, that there was some degree of legitimate combat that must have existed. But the Trial Chamber ignored this evidence and thus ignored this alternative reasonable -- this alternative conclusion reasonable under the evidence, in violation of in dubio pro reo. I'll remind Your Honours that the Prosecution the other day also kept saying: This judgement is reasonable. This judgement is reasonable. Your Honours, that's not the correct standard for a conviction to stand. It must be the only reasonable conclusion under the evidence, not just a reasonable conclusion under the evidence. There is no analysis in the trial judgement as to the acceptable margin of error for artillery shelling. There is no setting of a clear standard that would separate shelling due to legitimate military action and military necessity and one that is not. Unfortunately, Your Honours, as we all know, even legitimate military shelling can cause unintended collateral damage to property. But even more so, the Trial Chamber in volume 2, paragraph 353 confirms: "It has admitted evidence that the destruction, in particular, of houses in the town of Gornji Vakuf did not merely result from HVO shelling but also from fighting inside the city between HVO and ABiH and from shelling by the VRS." Your Honours, given such a finding, no Trial Chamber could thus conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the destruction in question was the result of indiscriminate or wilful and wanton acts of the HVO, let alone Mr. Coric. Now, Your Honours, we would like to address the tenth and last of your specific questions addressed to our Defence, which asks us to comment upon the potential impact upon the JCE 3 conviction of our client if you were to grant Ground 1(A) of the Prosecution's appeal. First of all, we note that granting of Prosecution's subground (A) of their appeal would not have any effect on the JCE 3 convictions that we are appealing from. I would direct Your Honours' attention first to paragraph 198 of our appellant's brief, where we specify that the "possibility" standard is the proper measure for JCE 3 and wherein we state that the Trial Chamber erred in applying that standard to conclude crimes were foreseeable to Coric because he did not have any knowledge to properly foresee that these crimes were possible as part of anything he intended. Additionally, we note that although the Trial Chamber admittedly does act in a sloppy manner linguistically, using terminology of probability and possibility, that as far as the additional crimes wherein Coric was convicted of JCE 3 liability, it is clear that the Trial Chamber actually already applied the correct possibility standard but applied it erroneously to find Coric guilty of those crimes which in fact he could not foresee under such a standard. For example, we would direct Your Honours to paragraphs 200, 207, and 209 of our appellant's brief for example. Now -- where we detail and describe the Trial Chamber's errors in applying the possibility standard to wrongfully convict Coric as to these additional crimes. I will point to just one example for the same of time. Volume 4, paragraph 1018, 1020, Coric is being erroneously convicted by the Trial Chamber for JCE 3 liability for killings in Dretelj precisely using the correct standard and the correct language "might be committed" to assess foreseeability. So, irrespective of your finding as to the Prosecution's appeal, Your Honours should acquit Mr. Coric of liability for all the JCE 3 crimes he is currently wrongfully convicted of. Further, as we have already detailed in the remainder of the paragraphs of Ground 8 of our appeal, under the evidence it is irrelevant if probability or possibility standards are applied because no reasonable Trial Chamber could find Coric guilty under JCE 3 using either standard, because he could not foresee crimes given the totality of the evidence that would go unpunished. Thus, the Prosecution's appeal has no relevance to our appeal from the wrongful convictions suffered by Mr. Coric for JCE 3 crimes. The Prosecution appeal submits that the appeals jurisprudence confirms that JCE 3 liability arises if the JCE members know that the commission of crime is a "possible" consequence of the execution of the common criminal purpose. Furthermore, in its appeal, the Prosecution states that the correct standard for JCE 3 mens rea means that the crimes "might be" perpetrated in executing the common criminal purpose and the accused willingly took that risk by deciding or continuing to participate in that enterprise; but Mr. Coric never participated in any enterprise. And however, as the Prosecution at paragraph 198 of its appeal highlights and indeed introduces precisely the reasonable doubt we're talking about as to Mr. Coric, they say: "By remaining in positions of authority, intending or aware of ongoing crimes committed ..." and then they continue, stating that he willingly took the risk that JCE 3 crimes might be committed. Respectfully given his police role, it is not enough to say as to Mr. Coric that he was aware of crimes. He also must have intended crimes, and the analysis shows he went to great lengths to try to prevent crimes, which is contrary to an intent to willingly take part in any crimes let alone any enterprise. We must stress again that the Sainovic appeals judgement, paragraph 1557, states that it must be foreseeable to the accused that the crimes might be committed - and this is the part I stress: "... in order to carry out the actus reus of the crimes forming part of the common purpose." As we have shown, Mr. Coric was never part of any common criminal purpose, and my colleague will deal with that more. The Prosecution alleges in subground 1(A) of its appeal that under the proper foreseeability standard Coric would be -- should be -- would be convicted, not acquitted as he was of certain crimes. But again, apart from using imprecise language, the Chamber appears to be applying the same possibility standard both when convicting and when acquitting Mr. Coric. The Coric Defence gave a very specific and detailed answer to subground 1(A) of the Prosecution's appeal in paragraphs 19 to 23 of its respondent's brief, and we would refer Your Honours to those as we stand behind them today. And we must stress again as I just read from paragraph 198 of their appeal, the Prosecution concedes reasonable doubt exists as to Coric's intent. If Coric was merely aware of crimes occurring within the territory, which is the common duty of every policeman in the world, and if he did not intend such crimes therefore he cannot be held responsible for them. In paragraphs 186 to 210 and elsewhere in our appeal brief, we cite to ample evidence that Coric could not even have known of certain events due to, for instance, for being hospitalised in Zagreb in a certain time-period and due to the military police being resubordinated to the HVO military and then also -- because he could legitimately interpret information that he was receiving as lawful combat and lawful application of the law on abandoned property. Likewise, in those same paragraphs, we clearly cite to numerous evidence that demonstrate that neither Coric nor the military police tolerated crimes and undertook actions to prevent the same and punish perpetrators. Coric's behaviour in acting against crimes therefore prevents any reasonable Trial Chamber from concluding that he willingly and knowingly took the risk that his acts or contributions to any legal effort might possibly lead to commission of crimes. One is in contradiction to the other. Further, he could not foresee the possibility of deaths that were never reported to him and were different in nature to those which occurred earlier which were in combat, as is the case with the deaths in Dretelj, for instance, and which we discuss in paragraph 208 of our appeal. We return to the simple fact that the Trial Chamber did not use the wrong standard, despite what the Prosecution alleges, besides the fact that the Trial Chamber linguistically was challenged and imprecise with the use of words "probability" and "crime would be committed" alongside "could" and "might be committed," the totality of the Chamber's findings must be taken into account. It is respectfully submitted that when the totality of the findings are considered, the Trial Chamber did not use the wrong standard and the acquittals were properly rendered in accord with the proper standard. In fact, the Trial Chamber cites in volume 1, paragraph 1 -- 216 to 217 as to the JCE 3 standard precisely some of the appeals jurisprudence that the Prosecution accepts as the correct standard in paragraph 30 of their appeal and also cites to the appeals jurisprudence that the -- that arises from the trial judgements that the Prosecution is relying upon as the proper standard. Further, we can -- further as to ground 1 of the Prosecution appeal -- 1(A) of the Prosecution appeal, we can say: Considering the statements of the Chamber in regards to the murders in Stolac and Capljina and for Dretelj prison, the Chamber utilised the proper analysis and the proper standard, such that these acquittals are also proper; namely, the consequence of the lack of evidence, not application of a wrong or different standard to weigh the evidence. So these acquittals would not be affected by any finding of accepting ground 1(A) of the Prosecution appeal. In -- one moment. In summation, apart from the occasional linguistic lapses in the use of the words "probable" and "would be" in passing and in dicta, the Trial Chamber actually applied and relied upon the possibility standard in its holding and rulings by its essence; and that is what the Prosecution admits by saying that the Chamber used this standard in the judgement "occasionally." The Prosecution is now just using verbal interpretation of expressions in paragraphs 216 and 220 of judgement and not a -- not the logical and systemic interpretation of law and the legal text cited by the Chamber in its findings. So the Prosecution's allegations are baseless. The Chamber used the correct standard as developed and applied by the relevant Appeal Chamber jurisprudence; and for this reason, we believe that subground 1(A) should not be granted of the Prosecution's appeal. For the foregoing reasons, the Coric Defence respectfully submits that criminal liability for additional JCE 3 crimes should not attach to Mr. Coric since they were not foreseeable to Coric even under the possibility standard because the information that he had at hand was not sufficient to put him on notice of the possibility of crimes, especially when in the hospital in Zagreb, and the fact that he did not intend any crimes in the first place. And further still, his actions undertaken to prevent crimes demonstrate he did not willingly and knowingly take part -- take the risk that crimes would occur, but rather fought against crimes at all times. I thank you and now my colleague will take over --

That is why I assert that the conclusions of the Trial Chamber regarding the responsibility of my client relating to prisons are not the only reasonable conclusions on the basis of admitted evidence which could not be challenged by other reasonable conclusions. Why is this important? It is important because these witnesses by their function had to have seen these documents at the time that they were drafted. What does this prove? It proves that these documents at the alleged time of their drafting did not exist.

Why does the Defence insist on a detailed analysis of these documents, both in relation to their contents and forms but also in the way that they correlate to other documents in the case? We insist, Your Honours, because it is very indicative that when we look at thousands and thousands of documents that the Trial Chamber looked at that are uncontested in relation to their signature and stamp - whose contents were confirmed by witnesses heard in the proceedings - they based their decision on Mr. Coric's responsibility on several documents which are the only ones without stamp or signature and whose authenticity and contents were not confirmed by a single witness and whose contents contradict the contents of these other valid documents and testimonies of witnesses heard in the proceedings. Your Honours, during the proceedings, the Defence tried in vain to find the log-books of documents received and dispatched of the military police administration. Regrettably, they have disappeared without a trace. Had they still been there, we could have had with 100 per cent certainty establish the credibility and authenticity of each document which allegedly originated from the military police administration. Still, even without those log-books - in a careful analysis of those documents individually and in correlation with other documents - at the very least it would have been possible to establish at that there was a reasonable doubt as to their authenticity. The Trial Chamber failed to carry out such an analysis and, for that reason, I assert that the Trial Chamber committed a serious mistake and it also constitutes a glaring example of a miscarriage of justice. The next error by the Trial Chamber I'd like to point it your attention to, Your Honours, is ignoring Defence evidence. The most drastic example of such treatment is Exhibit 5D04288. It concerns the log-books of registers of several courts and prosecutor's offices from the time and locations relevant to the indictment recorded on three CDs. Besides these registers, the register of the military court in Mostar was also admitted, Exhibit Number 5100 and P101. Your Honours, those registers contain hundreds of criminal reports submitted by the military police to the prosecutor's offices, they contain hundreds of proceedings conducted against known and unknown perpetrators for very diverse crimes committed against Muslims. After the Washington Agreement, the registers and measures registered therein were taken over by the competent courts and prosecutor's offices in the BH and continued working with them. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found Valentin Coric responsible because the perpetrators of these different crimes were not prosecuted and sentenced. And yet in paragraph 882 of volume 4, the Trial Chamber established that Coric, as the head of the military police administration, had the possibility to combat crime but his authority was limited to investigations, whereas prosecuting was in the hands of the except military prosecutor's office. Your Honours, these exhibits, these registers, prove that the military police did submit criminal reports to the competent authorities. Had the military police or the accused had the intention to incite crimes against Muslims, why would they have submitted reports against HVO members for such crimes? The finding of the Trial Chamber was that these crimes represent an integral part of the plan intended to further the criminal purpose, and Coric took part in it by trying to minimise the importance of serious crimes or failed to report, them that he failed to follow up on different investigations, and failed to prevent and sanction them. This finding by the Trial Chamber shows that it completely ignored the evidence which shows otherwise. Had the Trial Chamber considered and assessed such evidence, this conclusion would not have been possible. These registers, Your Honours, are crucial proof of this Defence; they that he that Valentin Coric did combat crime. From such evidence, it is clear that the Prosecutor did not, beyond reasonable doubt, prove their assertion that Coric intended that crimes against Muslims be committed and that they go unpunished. Except for ignoring documentary evidence, the Trial Chamber - without any plausible explanation - refused in part or in entirety the testimony of certain Defence witnesses, as discussed in detail in the paragraphs of appeal 301 to 303 and 305 to 308. The Trial Chamber refused to accept such testimony, irrespective of the fact that these witnesses testified in accordance with the documentary evidence on file and the testimony of other witnesses led by both other Defence teams and the Prosecution. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber without scrutiny accepted the testimony of Witness E, for example. For him there is indicia on the record testifying to his lack of credibility. He contradicted himself, he contradicted the testimony of other witnesses presented by the Prosecution as well as Defence as well as documentary evidence - the only instances in which the Trial Chamber did not admit or, rather, ignored his testimony where he confirmed the thesis of the Defence. Your Honours, ignoring such evidence amounts to another example of a miscarriage of justice at the expense of my client. The next error by the Trial Chamber I wanted to point out is the way the Trial Chamber assessed the authority of my client over the military police during the relevant time, thus assessing his contribution to the JCE. It was discussed in detail in Ground 2 paragraphs 39 to 58 of our appeal. For reasons of economy, I wanted to point out but several important errors. The Trial Chamber based its conclusions on Coric's effective control exclusively on his de jure authority, completely ignoring the de facto situation which was equally described by many witnesses on the Prosecution side as well as and the Defence side. Testimony of witnesses about the de facto situation runs counter to the conclusions of the Chamber about effective control. We can see that in volume 4, paragraphs 871, 872, 876, and 878 of the judgement and paragraphs 39 to 58 of our appeal. Despite such witness testimony, the Trial Chamber in its conclusions discusses a phantom dual chain of command and confusion in terms of command over the military police. The Trial Chamber reached this finding by misinterpreting witness testimony and dismissing such witness testimony that does not squarely fits this unfounded finding. To illustrate, I will point out an example of the Trial Chamber's erroneous finding. The Trial Chamber stated in its conclusions that the reforms conducted in the military police in July and December 1993 clarified the chain of command. In doing so, the Trial Chamber erroneously quoted Witness Biskic, saying that upon his departure the command chain was more transparent and the system of reporting was improved. But what did the witness actually say? Your Honours, Witness Biskic said that by December 1993 the units of the military police were withdrawn from the front line, enabling them to become more efficient, transcript pages 15181 and 15182. So this witness did not discuss any phantom dual chain of command. He simply said that the military police could not conduct its duties because it was engaged in fighting. Concerning this topic, I also wanted to draw your attention to certain contradictions in the judgement itself. When reading volume 4, paragraphs 624 to 628, and paragraphs 661 to 663, 816 to 818, 872, 876, and 878, what watch catches one's eye is that they are mutually contradictory and the findings tailored to fit the purpose, which was to establish liability for three different accused. Your Honours, the existence of several different commanders of the same rank in the same area commanding identical units is illogical and it is impossible to put into practice. It runs counter to military doctrine, especially in wartime conditions. In continuing, Your Honours, we will deal with the application of the principle in dubio pro reo in the findings of the Trial Chamber about the responsibility of Mr. Coric and his contribution to the JCE. I wanted to point your attention to paragraphs 1000, 1001 of volume 4. Your Honours, unlike the Trial Chamber, I believe there is a lot of evidence in the case that indicate there is at least one more reasonable inference on the evidence for each of these paragraphs. In this connection, we wish to draw your attention to just one example. I'll ask my colleague to show our first slide. That's a excerpt from document P5471, and that's the request by Mr. Coric to reconsider assigning military police units at the forward front lines addressed to several persons on 29 May 1993. My time is brief. I'm not going to read it. In any case, Mr. Coric requests his military policemen be returned to him because he hasn't enough men to fight crime and because they are assigned to front lines, they cannot conduct normal military police duties. In view of this, the logical question arises if Coric had the powers over the military police that the Trial Chamber decided he had, why didn't he simply command military policemen to withdraw? The answer is simple. Obviously he did not have the powers the Trial Chamber ascribed to him or, at the very minimum, there is a reasonable doubt because another reasonable inference imposes itself different to the one chosen by the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber accepts it's the only reasonable inference, the theory that Coric turned a blind eye to crimes and that they remained unpunished. I again remind you of the log-books mentioned at the beginning of my presentation. There is in this case file a large number of criminal reports, investigation documentation, and judgements; all these documents cast doubt on such findings. That's our appeal brief, paragraph 154 and 278. Now, we have a document P3571. This is a document that went out under the document -- under the name of Mr. Coric and speak to his attitude about crimes against Muslims in Mostar. In this document, Mr. Coric orders that these military policemen who committed the crime be relieved of duty, be dismissed from the police, and turned over to the prosecutor's office. Is this the conduct of a person who wants to let criminals go unpunished, somebody who wants to incite crime as the Trial Chamber concluded? We deal with the responsibility of Valentin Coric for detention centres in our appeal brief Ground 6 subgrounds (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h) and Ground 7, paragraphs 161 to 185. We have no time to elaborate. It's just one of the reactions of Mr. Coric after he received information ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From everything cited in these paragraphs, no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Mr. Coric failed to take every measure within his power or that he enabled bad treatment of prisoners. To conclude, Your Honours, I only want to mention regarding our 17th ground of appeal that in our entire appeal brief, we dealt with this in detail, that if the Appeals Chamber does not overturn the judgement and turn in the judgement of acquittal, at least the time spent in hospital should be reckoned as part of the sentence. The purpose of justice, Your Honours, is for justice to be done. Whether justice is done or not depends on -- does not depend on whether the accused goes free or to prison. The purpose of justice is for the guilty party to be declared guilty and an innocent man let go free. This is only possible with a guarantee of a fair trial and only if both parties have an equality of arms. That's why we ask you to remedy the errors made by the Trial Chamber, not only for the sake of our Defence but in the interests of international justice. This Defence suggests that you vary the trial judgement and bring a judgement of acquittal of Valentin Coric. My colleague tells me that I have five minutes left, so I would like to use them. Then I can -- then I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your colleague is perfectly correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will go back to this document that we have in front of us and then everything will make more sense. After learning that no significant change occurred at document --

utterances.text: Could the counsel please just let us find this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC

Paragraphs 141 and 142 of our appeal brief, footnotes 352, 353, and 354. Your Honours, I will turn back to the conclusion of my presentation. We were a bit confused towards the end because I'm looking at a different clock. And please, I appeal to you, Your Honours, once again to remedy the errors made by the trial to follow the principle of in dubio pro reo, fairness of proceedings, and equality of arms and bring a judgement of acquittal for Mr. Coric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, are you in a position to enlighten us on paragraph 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I may be, but I'd rather -- I have one document I'm missing. I'd rather want to see it with my own eyes, rather than to misrepresent something to you --
