utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I do have the information you requested that I did present before the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In response to your first question relating to paragraph 69 of the Prosecution's response, Your Honours, we would direct to paragraph -- pardon me, footnote 242 of that paragraph which cites to the Coric pre-trial brief in paragraph 75. That pre-trial was written by prior counsel and is not as eloquent as we would like, but we believe that it does present exactly the argument that we were making; and thus, the Prosecution is citing, on the one hand, the Coric's Defence objection to occupation and then arguing waiver. But we leave it for Your Honours to decide upon comparing the language of both with what the case actually is. In relation to the second matter you raised which was my citation to the response brief of the Prosecution at paragraph 73, I meant and should have referred Your Honours to the appellant appeal brief of the Prosecution, paragraph 227, wherein for foreseeability of murders, it talks only about not -- prior knowledge of murders and wilful killings in Gornji Vakuf, not other crimes, and that was the basis of these submissions that we made at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Prosecution, you have one hour and they we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President, Your Honours. Your Honour, Mr. Coric has presented a full and thorough Defence throughout his trial and again on appeal, he has presented comprehensive arguments including the detailed pleadings you've heard this morning. But it is our respectful submission that he fails to show any error in the trial judgement undermining his convictions and his arguments should be dismissed. Your Honours, Valentin Coric was a willing and significant participant in the joint criminal enterprise. As the chief of the military police administration, Coric should have been repressing crimes by HVO members. Indeed, that is a core function of the military police. It is perhaps their most important function. Instead, Coric used his position and his powers to contribute to the crimes against the Bosnian Muslims. He engaged military police in violent eviction and arrest operations which targeted Muslims en masse. He played a key role in the brutal detention network and deadly forced labour that Muslim detainees were subjected to over months and months. And he ordered the large-scale expulsion of Muslim detainees through so-called releases from detention. All the while Coric was shielding HVO perpetrators from criminal responsibility for their acts. He shielded them from responsibility for brutal expulsions of civilians from West Mostar in May, June, and later in 1993, and these were expulsions were Muslims were intimidated, beaten, robbed, and in some cases raped before being herded across the front lines. He shielded HVO members from responsibility for forced label, and as I've mentioned this was in some cases deadly, fatal for the Muslim detainees. Today the Defence hasn't mentioned these eviction operations from West Mostar. They haven't mentioned this forced labour programme, these deaths, this mutilation, this wounding of detainees during forced labour. And I'd like to you bear that in mind as I proceed with my submissions. Your Honours, Coric's actions and his lack of response in the face of these crimes, crimes which he was well-informed of was a cruel inversion of the duty that he owed to the citizens, the civilians, the Bosnian Muslims that he should have been protecting. On appeal, Coric has challenged almost every finding against him through his brief and as you've heard in his submissions today. He argues that he had no authority over the military police and detention camps, this despite orders and even reports drafted, issued by himself, showing that he did have such powers. He argues that news of crimes against Muslims did not reach him; however, he was informed and he was informed by multiple sources, by internationals, and by members of his own HVO. Many of these reports were addressed to him personally. Your Honours, confronted with exhibits showing his involvement, his deep implication in deadly forced labour and mass expulsions, these are crimes that are at the core of the joint criminal enterprise, he argues that they must be forgeries. And I'll address in due course the arguments that you heard concerning P3316 and P3320. Suffice to say at this point that the Trial Chamber dealt with these in the judgement and there are many other documents that build a web of corroborating evidence showing his role in these programmes. In relation to expulsions, for instance, can you see P4263, P4404, P10188, and P10187. That's just the tip of the iceberg. There are many more. Your Honours, his arguments do not stand up to scrutiny. The evidence against him is robust and mutually reinforcing. Instead of attempting to address all of his arguments, I will focus on two areas today; but I will cover the submissions that he has made this morning. I'll first address his arguments concerning his authority, particularly over the military police; and then I'll address his arguments concerning his willing contributions to the joint criminal enterprise. After that, I'll go through his arguments -- his responses to Your Honours' questions as set out in the Scheduling Order. Three notes. My references today will be to the trial judgement, unless otherwise indicated. I will refer to some materials that were testified to in private session, but I will not identify the source. And in relation to any arguments we do not cover, we rely on our written submissions. Before entering the substance of his arguments on authority, it's important to point out that many of his arguments are repetitions, often verbatim, of his trial arguments. As you noted at the outset of the hearing, this is not an opportunity for a trial de novo. His convictions have been properly entered. Your Honours, in some instances the record is misstated in Coric's arguments. For example, he argues at paragraph 162 of his brief: The Chamber even found Coric was not informed of mistreatment and had no reason to believe detainees were mistreated. However, the paragraph he cites, volume 4, paragraph 955, states the exact opposite. It finds Valentin Coric had reason to believe that the Heliodrom detainees were being mistreated during detention. And the Prosecution raised this in its response, paragraph 171, but Coric did not use the opportunity in his reply to clarify this point. Than are more examples. This is not to suggest any intentional misdirection, but it is to insist on a fair and accurate reading of the trial judgement. Turning to the first part of my submissions on Coric's authority over the military police. Your Honours, as you are well aware, this was not a short trial. Large amounts of evidence were submitted and not least in relation to command and authority over the military police. After reviewing the evidence at length, the Trial Chamber concluded that as chief of the military police administration, Coric had command and control over military police throughout his tenure. That's volume 4, paragraph 1000. And the Chamber's finding is well supported by the evidentiary record. At the outset, I would like to say a few words about the military police, who they were and what their role was in the JCE. The military police were recruited for their loyalty to the ideal of a Croatian homeland. That's volume 1, paragraph 848. By the end of 1992, there were over 2.000 military police, who were generally organised in battalions, each with hundreds of members. You can see that P956, page 7. The primary responsibilities of the military police were to: One, discover and combat crimes committed by or against HVO members; two, guard detainees; three, control freedom of movement using check-points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You can see this in volume 1, paragraph 888. However, during the joint criminal enterprise, the military police were centrally involved in many of the crimes. They participated in evicting Muslim civilians in operations in Gornji Vakuf, Mostar, Stolac, and Capljina, among others. They participated in the terrifying siege of East Mostar's desperate Muslim inhabitants. They abused Muslim detainees, thousands of them, in the Heliodrom, Dretelj, and Ljubuski detention centres. I've mentioned that they used Muslim detainees for perilous forced labour, and I've mentioned that they expelled thousands of Muslim detainees. As the Chamber rightly found, the military police were under Coric's authority. You can look, for example, to P956, page 3, which states: "Mr. Valentin Coric was appointed assistant commander of the security and information service and all existing military police units were placed under his command." It continues to state that in April 1992 military police stations were organised in 25 municipalities of Herceg-Bosna under the joint command of the military police administration. The Chamber's detailed nuanced findings as set out in volume 1, paragraphs 847 through 974, and volume 4, paragraphs 864 to 915. Now significantly Coric's power over the military police were not exclusive. The Trial Chamber found that there was a dual chain of command in operation, whereby HVO brigade commanders as well as the military police administration could, in certain instances, both exercise command over the military police. Coric argues that that finding was erroneous; however, it is well founded on the evidence. And you can see it in numerous exhibits, including reports from Coric himself, P957, page 5; as well as witness testimony at T22007. Now, Coric argues that he lost all power over the military police battalions when they were resubordinated -- the light assault battalion, I should say, which were just some of the military police, when they were resubordinated on 28 July 1993. However, the Trial Chamber properly dismissed this argument you can see at volume 1, paragraph 964 and 970. Its finding was well founded on the evidence. For example, on the slide you see P4010 this is an order from Coric to the 2nd Military Police Light Assault Battalion to deploy to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. What's important here is the date, that's 7 August, and you see it at the top of the document, 1993. That's after the 28 July resubordination order, in which Coric claims to have lost all powers over the light assault battalions. And note that this is signed by Zoran Suton. He is Coric's director of personnel and legal affairs, as shown in P5869. Coric issued many other orders after July 1993, after the point where he claims he had no authority. And these were orders to the military police, including light assault battalions. You see deployment orders such as P4151 from 13 August, sending military police to participate in activities in Mostar. Discipline orders concerning military police uniforms, P4126 on 12 August. Movement control orders, P5863 on 13 October, requiring the military police to stop and search a UNHCR convoy. Your Honours, in response Coric argues - and he's repeated this again today - that these are just de jure sources and they do not reflect the de facto situation on the ground. You heard that this morning. That is incorrect. There is a wealth of evidence showing that Coric's orders were enacted, they were implemented. For example, there's P2535, a report from the 4th Brigade Military Police of 27 May 1993, which states that the military police are transferring prisoners from Ljubuski to Heliodrom on the orders of Coric and Pusic. And the transfer took place as confirmed in P2546. In relation to P4010, which I just put on the slide, you can see that it was implemented as well. And that's shown in P4103, page 4, noting that the 2nd Light Assault Battalion indeed went to Mostar as ordered by Coric. Your Honours, the evidence clearly establishes that Coric's powers, his authority were recognised by those below him. The evidence also shows that those above him in the joint criminal enterprise in the power structures recognised his power and influence as well. For example, in October 1993, the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, was notified that the ICRC had complained about the treatment of detainees at Heliodrom prison. His response was to forward the report with a handwritten note to Coric, asking him to deal with the matter. P5792. These complaints were not minimal. The ICRC noted that the detainees had been severely beaten by some of the units which take people for work, and a number of detainees needed to be hospitalised for their injuries. Where there was a problem with the prison network, Mate Boban turned to Coric. Then in November 1993, when Coric was nominated to be minister of the interior of Herceg-Bosna, we see in a meeting between Franjo Tudjman and Jadranko Prlic a discussion where Prlic says: "For this position, we need the most forceful and authoritative individual." Prlic replied: "Coric absolutely is that." And he then explained that Coric enjoyed the general confidence of the army. That's P6581, pages 26 to 29. And Tudjman accordingly awarded Coric the position of minister of the interior. Your Honours, Coric fails to show that he had no powers over the military police and that he could not exercise his influence in any way. Turning to the arguments concerning Coric's significant contributions to the JCE, he has challenged this at length in his brief and touched on this in his pleadings today. Your Honours, Coric deployed military police units for mass eviction and arrest operations and he equipped them with hundreds of thousands of bullets, thousands of grenades, and other equipment. See volume 4, paragraph 1000, and P3090, page 27. He was an architect of the network of brutal detention centres, per volume 4, paragraph 982. He ignored repeated reports that Muslim detainees were being wounded and killed while engaged in work on the front lines, volume 4, 971. And he himself authorised detainees to work on the front lines, unlawful labour. He sent troops to assist in the siege of East Mostar, while also cutting off humanitarian aid to worsen the situation of the desperate Muslim inhabitants. And as I've mentioned, he played a key role ordering mass expulsions of detainees, Muslim detainees. But I'll look first to one of his central contributions to the JCE which is his failure to fight crimes by HVO members. Your Honours, again here his arguments repeat his trial submissions, often verbatim, and we've noted that, for instance, in the response brief, paragraph 41. He fails to show the Trial Chamber acted unreasonably in reaching this finding and this finding that he did, in fact, ignore crimes and failed to take the proper response, the proper measures in response to these crimes. In fact the Trial Chamber held that he turned a blind eye to vicious crimes and one example that I want to refer to is that of the evictions in East Mostar. Your Honours, these evictions, the ones in June 1993, involved HVO soldiers, including members of the Vinko Skrobo antiterrorist group, subjecting Muslims to intimidation, threats, and beatings, confiscating their property, raping Muslim women, and sending them across the front line to East Mostar. See volume 2, paragraph 872 to 876. Coric was informed of these violent expulsions. He was informed by internationals, volume 2, paragraph 873. And you'll also see in military police administration records accounts of these evictions in which they call them ethnic cleansing. See volume 2, again paragraph 873, and the evidence cited therein. So how did Coric react to this information? To the internationals he tried to brush the problem away. He said, paraphrasing: It didn't happen; and if it happened, then it was done by people they didn't have under control, criminals or whatever. You'll see that transcript page 21047 to 21048. But these were not out-of-control elements. In fact, it was members of the HVO 3rd Brigade and the Skrobo anti-terrorist group who were also under the command of the HVO, volume 1, paragraph 818 and 829, carrying out these crimes. One would expect the top military policeman's reaction to this news to be quick and severe. Instead, Coric 's approach was accommodating, both metaphorically and literally. For a start, the perpetrators were not arrested or punished, volume 2, paragraph 898, and P3666. But it went further. Coric specifically instructed his military police to disregard crimes by these perpetrators. We have in evidence a report, P3928, from the Military Police Crime Department that was part of the military police administration. In it, the author complains that Coric ordered his department to not investigate certain crimes committed by the Vinko Skrobo anti-terrorist group, as the Chamber sets out in volume 4, paragraphs 931 to 933. Even further than this, Coric consented to members of the HVO military police moving into the houses, the apartments of evicted Muslims in West Mostar. See volume 4, para 929, and P2879, and transcript page 25421. You will also see this pattern of Coric allowing HVO members to move into apartments of evicted, expelled Muslims occur in October. Look at P6232, P5554, P5518, and transcript page 17208. Coric's failures and his reaction, his accommodating reaction to these crimes had severe implications for the Bosnian Muslim inhabitants of Mostar and throughout these territories. The same Skrobo anti-terrorist group continued to commit vicious crimes against Muslims which included expulsions, thefts, rapes in Mostar in September 1993, sometimes committed together with members of the military police. They also caused detainees, Muslim detainees, to be used as human shields. You see this in volume 3, paragraph 727, 782, and 933. Your Honours, there is plenty more evidence of this nature. The Trial Chamber acted reasonably in concluding that Coric contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by protecting HVO members from responsibility for their crimes against Bosnian Muslims. Now, Coric has claimed today that he did, in fact, submit reports and that he was attempting to do what he could in the circumstances. However, the Trial Chamber has addressed these arguments, it's looked into the details, and it's rightly, properly concluded that he failed to do so where he was informed of crimes by HVO members against Bosnian Muslims going to the core of this JCE, evictions in West Mostar, forced labour, detention crimes. You'll see in volume 1, paragraph 918 to 919, that the Trial Chamber addressed these arguments. And you'll also see that despite the fact that there were criminal reports being submitted, these were primarily for crimes attenuated distinct from the crimes at the core of this JCE, crimes like car theft, tax evasion. You see this in P4699, page 24 to 25. When you look at the category of crimes against the civilian population, genocide, terrorism, the crimes that we are addressing at page 26, it notes - this is P4699 - that the reports sent to the military prosecutor, these are the reports from the military police, were exclusively against Serbs and Muslims who victimised Croats. There is a mention of other crimes being prosecuted but no mention of crimes against Muslims such as brutal forced labour, such as mass expulsions, and such as evictions. Where are those crimes? What was being done for those victims? Your Honours, there are more examples. P3616, page 4, in a meeting with military police personnel, 21 July 1993, the military prosecutor, Jurisic stated: "We are now overloaded with charges of failure to respond to mobilisation orders, overloaded with charges against war criminals and also charges against members of the Muslim armed forces, but there are no charges against criminals in the town of Mostar." And as we just saw, the serious charges against civilian population, the war crimes types of charges, were not being charged for crimes against Bosnian Muslims by HVO members. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber built its conclusions on a solid foundation of evidence and Coric has failed to show that it acted unreasonably. He has also argued today that he made requests for the military police to return from the front lines to enable him to do his job. And he has cited P5471 and P6837. Again, the Trial Chamber took this into account. It addressed it in volume 1, paragraph 972. And what Coric omits to mention is that he was the one who had deployed the military police to the front lines. In accordance with his role as a member of the a JCE involving multiple people, he carried out his function. He sent the military police to repeated eviction operations that I've mentioned. And it's also significant that these requests he has referred to today are from September and November 1993. This is very late in the game, Your Honours. But it's also at a time when Coric continued to deploy military police to the front lines, including to Gornji Vakuf, 29 September 1993, that's P5478; and to Mostar, where he himself had personally visited the front lines and seen the crimes that were occurring, seen the results of the crimes. That's P5657 from 5 October 1993. In many instances, Your Honours, it was the military police committing the crimes, bringing more back would have simply led to more crimes against Muslims, and this was a result of the culture that Coric fostered in the military police units. For instance, you see this manifested in a report on activities in Prozor, 1993. P4177. This is a HVO report. It says: "The military police are implementing an order from a higher level to detain Muslims between the ages of 16 and 60 in their own particular way, imprisoning men without exception, including those younger than 16 and older than 60, and treating them in an extremely inhumane manner." It notes that together with local soldiers, the military police were involved in crimes, including murdering Muslim prisoners, stealing their property, and raping and humiliating female Muslims, forcing them to strip in front of their fathers and forcing their fathers to strip in front of them. That's at pages 2 to 3 of P4177. Your Honours, it's this culture, it's this trend, it's this pattern that led one international who dealt with the military police to describe them as the most counter-productive and radical in the field and he described people commanding the military police as quite clearly radicals. That's transcript page 25818, 25819. Your Honours, turning to Coric's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise through the detention network and forced labour. The Trial Chamber found on a thorough review of the evidence that Coric enjoyed extensive powers over the detention network. He established the Heliodrom and Ljubuski prisons and had direct authority over their wardens. He was responsible for the security of detainees at Heliodrom, Dretelj, and Ljubuski. He authorised the use of prisoners for forced labour, and he had the power to order these so-called releases, in reality expulsions, of Muslim detainees. Coric denies many aspects of his authority. For instance, he claims he did not order the establishment of Heliodrom. However, the Trial Chamber's finding at volume 2, paragraph 1394, was securely established on the evidence. For example, there's P6805, this is a military police administration report which states that the military detention facility in Mostar, that's Heliodrom, was relocated to Heliodrom on the orders of the military police chief and that was Coric at the time. His denial of that authority, of those powers was properly rejected. And it's important to understand the context, the significance of his denial of this authority, of his denial of this role. He received repeated information about the deplorable conditions of prisoners and detainees. And I've mentioned that earlier, the note from Boban to Coric about serious mistreatment. One of the worst forms of mistreatment that is at issue today and which I have referred to is forced labour. And Coric was regularly informed that Heliodrom detainees were being mistreated, wounded or killed while working on the front lines. That's volume 4, paragraphs 955, 966, 1001. Now, what was this forced labour, what did it consist of? Well, it was described by witness Mujo Copelj who said that when he was detained at Heliodrom, the HVO soldiers took him and other detainees in groups of 30 to the front lines. The HVO soldiers forced the Muslim detainees at gunpoint to run out into exposed areas and each detainee had to place at least five sandbags on the defence line. As the prisoners did so, bullets rained down on them from the other side. Some detainees were killed, and many were wounded, while Copelj looked on. Many other witnesses gave similar accounts, for example, volume 2, 1602. Now, Coric argues again that he had no power to authorise or approve the use of detainees for work. And, again, his denial of power is incorrect. It's false. For example, if you look at P4039 which we place on the slide, this is an order from Petkovic on 8 August 1993 and it's sent to various HVO brigade commanders. At point 1, Petkovic states: "Immediately carry out maximum fortification of lines reached. You may uses prisoners and detained Muslims to fortify the lines. Seek the necessary approval from the military police department (which is in charge of utilisation of prisoners)." Numerous reports were submitted to Coric detailing the results, the brutal and often deadly results of this forced labour. For example, on 4 August 1993, he is told that Muslim detainees were beaten up when taken from Heliodrom for work by the HVO 3rd Brigade. P3939. On 16 August, he is told that one prisoner was killed and three wounded when taken from Heliodrom to do forced labour. P4221. And then we see on the slide a report, P5008, of 13 September 1993, another report, and there are many more of these, which notes in the bold part: "While carrying out their work obligations, 50 prisoners were wounded while six were killed by the Muslim armed forces. While groups of HVO soldiers took prisoners home and thereby made it possible for them to visit their families, some of our other soldiers mistreated the prisoners. In our reports 522/93 of 4 August and 524/93 of 7 August, you have been informed of the mistreatment of prisoners of the 2nd Battalion of the 2nd Brigade and anti-aircraft defence of Siroki Brijeg." Importantly, this report which is from the warden of the Heliodrom prison, Stanko Bozic, goes on to inform Coric that, if we move to the next excerpt: "On 10 August, the International Committee of the Red Cross came to visit the prison. They worked for three days, registering all the detainees and prisoners. The representative of the ICRC, Mr. Franco Faoro, discussed with the prison warden the question of the inadequate conditions of solitary confinement cells, the quality and quantity of food and its improvement, and the fact that detainees go to work on the front line (forbidden under the Geneva Conventions) ..." Coric argues that these reports of the Heliodrom warden were not sent to him or the military police administration, and this repeats his trial argument again. That was properly dismissed at trial, and you can see that because many of these reports are addressed to him personally. And you can see that on this report, for example, at the bottom in the address tag. Additionally, reports detailing the same mistreatment come from multiple sources. There's a report on 30 September 1993 from the 5th Military Police Battalion and that said that Heliodrom prisoners were taken to work at the front line, were sometimes wounded or mutilated, and sometimes did not return at all. It's P5497. That was also sent to Coric personally as you can see at page 16. There are many more examples listed in the judgement such as at volume 2, footnote 3754. Coric's claims of ignorance about this practice are false but they're also telling. So how did Coric react to this information? Well, as the Trial Chamber found, he did nothing to prevent the practice and, in fact, he allowed it to continue, and he authorised it himself. We have evidence showing that in August he authorised Muslim prisoners from Vitina Otok, that's a different HVO prison. He authorised these prisoners to taken for forced labour at the front lines as set out in trial judgement volume 4, paragraph 977. Now, the evidence doesn't tell us the fate of those specific prisoners, but it does tell us they were sent to the front lines and it does tell us that Coric was authorising and signalling his approval of this practice. Far from preventing it, far from repressing it, as he was supposed to do. Your Honours, these reports about forced labour, particularly the ones from Stanko Bozic, plead to Coric to take measures. When you look at them, you can see him requesting again and again for intervention. He is asking Coric to do what Coric was required to do as the chief military policeman. Coric did not. And in the meanwhile, dozens of Muslim detainees were killed, hundreds were wounded and traumatised. His claim of ignorance is a facade that was properly rejected at trial. Your Honours, the third and final contribution that I'll address is his involvement in this mass displacement, this industrial-scale displacement of Muslim detainees from the detention network. Through the system, detainees with letters of guarantees from third countries were requested -- were released - sorry - from the brutal prisons and given a short time, sometimes hours, to leave Herceg-Bosna, and they were required to leave with their families. This was an organised means of expelling Muslims en masse. After assessing the evidence in detail, the Trial Chamber found that Coric ordered and facilitated expulsion through this process. Volume 4, paragraph 982. And its finding is well supported by the evidence. For example, in August 1993, Coric issued an order for the release of Muslims from Ljubuski who had letters of guarantee, Muslim detainees, I should say. These Muslim detainees who were subject to Coric's order were given 24 hours to leave their homes and to depart to a third country and had to leave with their families. This is noted in volume 2, paragraph 1644, and you see also in transcript page 22095. Pursuant to Coric's order, detainees were expelled from Heliodrom, Vitina Otok, Ljubuski, Dretelj and Gabela prisons. Coric's response in his arguments is complete denial. You've heard him today say that he had no power to release prisoners, referring to P3316-P3320. Your Honours, that is incorrect and it is shown to be incorrect by a wealth of evidence. For example, we can look at P10191 which is on the slide and you will see here that it says: "In accordance with the law and pursuant to the order of the chief of the military police, Mr. Valentin Coric, we ask the command of Heliodrom in Mostar to release the people of Muslim ethnicity who possess letters of guarantee. The detainees: Fadil Maksumic, born in 1955, Ismet Micijevic, born in 1956, Admir Osmic, who are detained in the military prison Heliodrom in Mostar should be handed over to the military police in Ljubuski because their families are in Ljubuski and are being exiled from Croatia." Exiled, Your Honours. There are many more examples. I listed some of them at the outset of my submissions. Your Honours, Coric knew that these expulsions through releases affected a huge number of Muslim detainees and Muslim people in general. For example, he knew that in Dretelj alone there were over 2.000 Muslims that had been detained through mass arrest campaigns in Capljina. That's volume 4, paragraphs 985 to 986, and 993. Expelling them, together with their families, would clearly have a huge impact on the psyche, the morale, the existence of the Muslim population of Herceg-Bosna. Coric argues that even if he was involved in these releases, it was for the prisoners' own good. That's at paragraph 180 of his appeal brief. Effectively he is saying he was improving their lot by releasing them from these deplorable, horrific conditions. What he omits to mention is that it was the HVO, including the military police in many instances, who were committing the vicious crimes, who were responsible for the deplorable, horrific conditions in these detention centres, and it was these conditions that led the Muslim detainees wanting to leave. The prisoners suffered in overcrowded, insanitary conditions. Cramped together, they had to take turns to lie down to sleep. Some prisoners received so little water they had to drink their own urine. You see that volume 3, paragraph 1124. And each day they woke up to the prospect of being selected for forced labour, effectively Russian roulette with their lives. The terror and desperation is hard to imagine. Your Honours, that is the context in which these prisoners chose to be released, if you could call it a choice at all. And Coric was well aware of those conditions. The Trial Chamber assessed and validly concluded that the prisoners did not enjoy genuine choice in these circumstances, and it properly concluded that this was a means of expulsion. See volume 2, paragraph 1648; volume 3, paragraph 817. You've seen the orders showing that Coric played a key role in this industrial-scale expulsion. It was validly taken into account as a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, I will now turn to your questions as set out in the Scheduling Order, and I'll focus first on question 4, which, as you are aware, concerns the impact on the scope and the convictions under the joint criminal enterprise, particularly for murder if the murder and wilful killing conclusions related to Dusa in Gornji Vakuf were to be reversed. As you've already heard in relations to parts A and B of your question, overturning these convictions related to Dusa would have no impact on the scope of the common criminal plan, nor on the mens rea under JCE 1 for murder of the appellants, and that applies in the same respect for Coric. There were many murders under this joint criminal enterprise. Removing one incident would have no impact. So, Your Honours, I'll focus on question 4(c), concerning the third category of joint criminal enterprise. And here you've asked and heard about two documents, P1393, P1414. Now, the short answer is that there would be no impact on Coric's convictions and there would be no impact that would undermine the Prosecution's appeal in which it seeks further JCE 3 convictions for murder. If we look first to the JCE 3 convictions that were entered against Coric, these were for two killings of Muslim detainees in the Dretelj detention centre in August 1993. That's set out in volume 4, paragraph 1017. The Trial Chamber took an extremely restrictive approach in its analysis of joint criminal enterprise 3 mens rea, a compartmentalised approach, and the Prosecution has submitted this is an error as set out in its appeal brief and as you will hear in our appeal submissions. But even on this strict approach, it nonetheless found the evidence was sufficient for these two murders in Dretelj in August 1993. Why was this? Well, this was because he had actual knowledge of other killings of Muslim detainees in the same detention centre in July, just weeks before these murders. Your Honours, this is sufficient notice to put anyone on alert of the risk, the foreseeability that further murders might be perpetrated. Anyone, let alone the chief of the military police administration who was centrally involved in this network of detention centres. Your Honours, you'll see the references in volume 4, paragraph 1018. If we look now and I see -- I see the time. And I could suggest -- I'm about to turn to a new subtopic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I will continue. Thank you. If we look now to the additional JCE 3 murders for which Coric, according to the Prosecution, should have been convicted, you'll see that these concern eviction-related murders, detention-related murders as set out in Prosecution appeal brief paragraph 242. In many of these cases, the Trial Chamber simply forgot to adjudicate Coric's individual criminal responsibility under JCE 3. And for these, the evidence would remain entirely sufficient to convict him even if the Dusa killings were removed. This is because, first, of his willing participation in this joint criminal enterprise, this violent, ethnically animated campaign against Bosnian Muslims which involved the deliberate use of extreme violence. And it is also because of the repeated notice he got of serious violent crimes against Muslims. Looking to the first point, his role in the -- his participation, I should say, in the JCE. As mentioned, the criminal campaign at the heart of the JCE involved serious violent crimes, including murder. I've set out at length Coric's role in the eviction operations, detention crimes, and vicious murders of detainees used for forced labour and as human shields. Coric also contributed to the crimes in East Mostar, which included murder. He had an office in central Mostar at the time and visited the front line. See volume 4, paragraph 936, and transcript page 18341. He knew of the shelling and fire campaign, but nonetheless sent military police units to assist the siege, and he cut off humanitarian supplies to the desperate, trapped Muslim inhabitants. Volume 4, paragraph 937 to 943. Coric's role, his participation and his involvement in this campaign of extreme violence, violence committed on an ethnic basis, is clearly relevant to his JCE 3 mens rea. And the Appeals Chamber has confirmed the relevance of these factors to an accused's joint criminal enterprise 3 liability and that they may be taken into account. In the Sainovic appeals judgement, for instance, paragraphs 1089, 1591. Your Honours, Coric, as I've mentioned, received repeated reports of serious violence against Muslims, specific notice of crimes. I see the time and if this is convenient, I will pause submissions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It certainly is. We will break now and we will resume at 2.30. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours. At the outset, a couple of corrections for the transcript to verify that it is accurate and that I did not misspeak. At transcript page 54, P5689 was recorded and I meant to say P5869. At transcript page 61, where I cited volume 1, para 972, I should have also cited volume 1, para 940. And when I referred to two exhibits, P3316 and P3320, I should have said P3216 and P3220. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Returning to my submissions before the break, Your Honours, I mentioned that Coric repeatedly received notice about violent crimes, including violent crimes against Muslims by HVO members. I'll look first to the documents that you've specifically highlighted in your questions, P1393 and P1414, concerning joint criminal enterprise 3. Your Honours, P1393 is a report from 2nd February 1993 from Berislav Pusic and others in the crime police department of Coric's military police administration, and it recounts that the Tomislavgrad military police had beaten and robbed detainees in Ljubuski. The victims were left with visible wounds and bruises. Your Honours, the following day, Coric issues P1414, and here he merely calls for a report into the circumstances and that the property taken from the prisoners be given to the military police administration. The Defence has argued that this indicates he took effective adequate measures in the response, the appropriate measures in response to news of serious violence. Well, the first point, Your Honours, is that this issue, JCE 3, is about notice. Having learned of this serious violence, you can't unring the bell, Your Honours. He doesn't lose that awareness. But also, when we look at the record, there's reason to doubt that he did take serious measures in response to these reports. Your Honours, the report itself does not mention punishing the military police, and what we do know is that the commander, the overall commander of these military police, Zdenko Andabak, was appointed to a higher position a few days later, 10 February 1993, on Coric's recommendation. We also know that Coric permitted the Tomislavgrad military police, the same unit that severely beat these detainees in Ljubuski, to continue to guard detainees in 1993. You can see these in P1460 and P3551. Moreover, Your Honours, this was not the first time Coric was learning of the criminal propensity of the Tomislavgrad military police. In October 1992, he had been informed of the crimes and ill discipline by the Tomislavgrad military police under Zdenko Andabak and he was asked to take measures against them. The Trial Chamber assessed this evidence and found that he failed to do so. That's at volume 4, paragraphs 1246 to 1252. And that's the basis for his Article 7(3) responsibility prior to the commencement of the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, the Defence has referred to the evidence of Zdenko Andabak, transcript page 50953, in arguing that Coric fostered a stringent culture in the military police. Well, first, the Trial Chamber assigned little weight to Andabak's evidence in relation to these crimes in October 1992 as you will see in volume 2, para 59. You'll also see that this continuity in the perpetrators, the identity of the perpetrators, is matched by a continuity of inadequate response by Coric, and it's also matched by a continuity of crimes and even an escalation of crimes to more serious crimes, Your Honours. The key point for his joint criminal enterprise 3 mens rea is that he was aware of the risk, the possibility of serious violence against Bosnian Muslims in the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, he was, as you know, found to be aware of the violence, extreme violence committed during the operations in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. He also received numerous reports referring to crimes, including murders, and including against Muslims. He knew of the violent evictions in Mostar in May 1993. You see these in volume 4, paragraphs 926 to 928. Your Honours, these evictions were brutal, Muslims were kicked punched and hit with rifle-butts. HVO soldiers threatened to kill the Muslims and pointed their guns at families with young children. That's volume 2, paragraph 822. There is a report from 9 June concerning Prozor, P2697. You see at page 3 Coric - and this is addressed to Coric - that he is informed of crimes including murder, arson, and looting. He is informed that the military police have released murderers. He has released -- he is informed that one prisoner was killed and that there have been other incidents. There's additional evidence showing that in mid-1993 Coric knew that the HVO was holding Muslim detainees in Prozor. And that's set out in volume 4, paragraph 998. And, Your Honours, the involvement of the military police in crimes in Prozor was notorious. I have mentioned P4177, a report that outlines the military police involvement in rapes, murders, and mistreatment of Muslims. In mid-July 1993, a representative of an international organisation protested to Coric through a series of meetings and he protested about evictions, looting, destruction of property, and the general campaign against Muslims across the affected territories. Although Coric said that steps would be taken, none ever materialised. That's transcript page 18340 through 18344. You can look at P4058, a report from Coric's military police administration that the Defence has referred to this morning. That shows he was informed of forced evictions and the murders of numerous Muslims, liquidations of Muslims. Simply put, Your Honours, Coric had abundant notice. He had notice that would put any person on alert of crimes, serious violence, including murders, against Muslims in the perpetration of the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, have asked about -- a question who was privy to the contents of a report by Zeljko Siljeg, P1351, of 29 January 1993. And as you've heard, that report describes killings and destruction that occurred during the Gornji Vakuf operation. It's our submission that Coric would have also received the information in that report. Along with Petkovic, Coric was tasked with implementing the Gornji Vakuf operation. P1140. Although he was not physically present during the operation, he has said that he was in overall command of the military police sent to Gornji Vakuf. P1053. And he reports after the operation, volume 4, paragraph 921 to 923. Your Honours, he was aware of this violence in Gornji Vakuf. He knew about the violent campaign against Muslims, and he contributed to it in multiple ways, through the brutal forced labour, through the expulsions, and through many other crimes. I should say he contributed to many other crimes committed as part of the JCE. This readily satisfies the mens rea standard under Your Honours' jurisprudence, and he should be convicted for the additional JCE 3 murders as set out in our appeal. Turning very briefly to question 5 that you have heard from the Defence on this morning. This concerns the destruction in villages in Gornji Vakuf. You will hear our submissions about this next week, on Tuesday. Essentially, we argue that this was wanton, unjustified destruction. There was a pattern in the crimes and the destruction, and you will see that in the villages the HVO soldiers torched houses. There's no military justification for burning down civilian houses. A brief word on question 10, Your Honours, that was touched on this morning. Your Honours, again, you'll hear more about this in the Prosecution appeal on Tuesday. But the bottom line is that many of Coric's arguments would be undermined by applying the correct standard for JCE 3 mens rea, which is the possibility standard, not the probability standard. For example, you'll see in his brief at paragraph 187 concerning Gornji Vakuf that he argues that it was an error to find -- or that the Prosecution has not shown, I should say, that he knowingly took the risk acts of theft would be committed. That's the probability standard he is applying. In Mostar, paragraph 199 of his brief, again, he says knowingly took the risk that acts of theft would be committed. And Coric could reasonably have foreseen that the HVO members would commit acts of sexual violence. So his arguments would be affected, Your Honours. Turning now to the issue of occupation that was raised this morning. Your Honours, he has failed to show any error in the trial judgement. In arguing that the HVO could not occupy its own territory, the Defence overlooks that this is occupation by agency. It is Croatia that is the occupying power. And you'll see this volume 3, footnote 1175. Again, contrary to the Defence arguments, a state of occupation does not require and does not hinge on there being an invasion. As set out in Article 2.2 of the Fourth Geneva Convention: "The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a High Contracting Party, even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance." And you've heard detailed submissions on the law on this issue previously. Additionally, that Croatia sometimes supported the ABiH with weapons does not undermine Croatia's overall control of the HVO as this related to times or areas other than those that we're concerned with in this case. Moreover, as you have seen previously this week, the presidential transcripts show repeatedly Croatia's control over the HVO and show that it went beyond providing mere weaponry, that it included organising these forces as well. Your Honours, Croatia was properly found to have been involved in organising and planning the military operations in BiH against the ABiH for the HVO. This meets the test required under our jurisprudence. Turning to the joint criminal enterprise existence challenges that have been raised, Your Honours, the Defence first addressed the Law on Joint Criminal Enterprise and asked Your Honours to reverse course midstream, we would say, to change the law on JCE. And they referred to the United Kingdom Supreme Court case of Jogee. The Defence argued, at transcript page 7 today, that the Appeals Chamber in Tadic relied on English case law in reaching its finding that there exists a valid legal doctrine of joint criminal enterprise in this Court's jurisdiction. However, in reality, the Tadic Appeals Chamber relied on customary international law in formulating JCE, and in contrast, it found that it could not rely on domestic provisions in order to determine common purpose liability. And you will see that in paragraphs 195 through 226 of the Tadic appeals decision. Your Honours, the Defence points to paragraph 224, footnote 287, in its argument that the Appeals Chamber relied on English law. But actually in that footnote, this -- the citation to English law is one of many which the Appeals Chamber summarised before concluding that these provisions cannot be relied on as a source of international principles or rules under the doctrine of the general principles of law recognised by the nations of the world because of the lack of a common approach across different legal systems. And since Jogee, Your Honours have issued the Stanisic and Zupljanin appeals decision which again confirmed the validity of joint criminal enterprise. You see that, for example, in paragraph 974. As to the existence of the joint criminal enterprise, the Defence has missed, has not addressed the core of the Trial Chamber's analysis in its arguments in pointing to assistance of arms, in claiming there was no pattern of crimes, because the evidence underlying these findings is clear and compelling. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May I be excused to go pick up some documents that we're printing. We have no one in the back to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me start with the words of one well-placed international witness who said the Bosnian Croats wanted to make it so that provinces 8 and 10 would have the greatest majority possible of Bosnian Croats. For them, it was about expelling from such provinces, the Bosnian Serbs and those they called the Muslims, the Bosnian Muslims. Transcript page 17535, cited at volume 4, paragraph 15. And provinces 8 and 10 contain the municipalities in which the vast majority of the crimes that we're addressing occurred. Another well-placed witness who you will be familiar with, Ambassador Herbert Okun explained the double game being played by the Bosnian Croat leadership. He said, referring to 1993: "In January, yes, the Bosnian Croats had signed the agreement and, yes, they were conducting ethnic cleansing operations in Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. They were doing both." That's cited in volume 4, paragraph 45. And, Your Honours, the evidence substantiates the pattern of crimes, crimes including murder, that were part of the JCE. For instance, in relation to these evictions, Your Honours, you will see that the victims included families, a woman doing her laundry, this is in Mostar when the attack started, a sick elderly man, and the HVO soldiers forced them to run across the front lines. They had gun-fire behind them from the HVO and gun-fire in front of them from the ABiH who didn't know who they were. Your Honours, what military purpose did these crimes serve? It's none. What they do serve is the purpose behind the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, I can refer to the demographics that you've heard of and there's two points in this connection. Firstly, the JCE crimes resulted in large-scale expulsion of the Muslim population; and, secondly, that these expulsions reflected the words of JCE members. If we look at the numbers, they largely speak for themselves. As the Trial Chamber observed at paragraph 57 of volume 4, there were dramatic falls in the numbers of Muslims in September and October 1993, which is when the JCE was well into its operation. Most strikingly, the population of Stolac, the Muslim population, I should say, went from 8093 to 0. Your Honours have heard about the statements from JCE members. You've heard Mate Boban's statement from 27 December 1991 about cleansing border areas. You've heard Praljak's statement, September 1992, about Muslim refugees and "unless we evict those people from there, we will not have a majority there." That's volume 4, paragraph 522. And you've heard Praljak's statement about homogenisation and that was made at a meeting on 2 April 1993 that Coric attended. Praljak said: "Now we have got what we want. The homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state. It is all as clear as noon on a spring day." That's P1788. Your Honours, the Defence have not addressed this key evidence going to the core of the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. Ultimately, Your Honours, Coric was informed and he was informed repeatedly about HVO crimes against Muslims. He was the chief of the military police administration and his core job was to address crimes by HVO members. Time and time again, he was silent in the face of serious crimes. He was silent in the face of the mistreatment of Mujo Copelj and the many other victims of forced labour at the front lines. And he was silent in the face of the expulsion of victims from Ljubuski and the exile of their families. Why was he silent? Why didn't the dog bark? Well, the reason is that he was contributing, he was a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. He was deploying military police for these operations in which large-scale crimes occurred. He was participating, facilitating mass arrest of Muslims, indiscriminate arrests. He was participating to the brutal detention network and the mistreatment and killing, the murder, of Muslims during forced labour. And ultimately, he was ordering the mass expulsion of Muslims including from the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna. Your Honours, Coric has not showed that his trial was unfair or that there was no reasonable basis for his conviction. The Trial Chamber gave a full hearing to his arguments, and he has failed to show any error and he has failed to show that his convictions should be overturned. Unless Your Honours have any questions, that would conclude my submissions. Much thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It hits you much before you expected. You have half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are ready to go. At the outset of my presentation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the outset of their presentation, the Prosecution stated that the Defence was repeating itself. Your Honours, partially they are correct. Our arguments were repeated because as of day one of the proceedings, we have been saying the same thing, as opposed to the Prosecution who have been adjusting their arguments depending on developments. I will show this by providing two examples. First, when Prosecutor addressed command responsibility with regard to Mr. Coric and resubordinating the units of the military police as well as his request that the military police be withdrawn from the front line. In that context, the Prosecutor stated two things. The first one was that Mr. Coric was waiting for September, then for November, to react. The other thing they said was that he did not lose his authority and that he was still in command. As regards the first Prosecution argument, it is clear that Mr. Coric could not have asked for the military police to be withdrawn from the front lines before November because that's when he became the minister of the interior. Until that day, he had nothing to do with the civilian police. The second argument, that Mr. Coric asked for that as late as of September, is not correct. In the introductory part of their arguments and in document P5471 we can read: We did warn against this on several occasions including this request. Meaning that the request from September was not the first of its kind by Mr. Coric. As regards the adjustment of their arguments, depending on what suited them best at any given moment, we wish to remind you of paragraph 742 and 748 of the Prosecution final brief where they state that another accused made Coric's request impossible to meet and that this other person was responsible for the fact that the military policemen were kept at the front lines. Furthermore, the Prosecutor implied that the personnel policy of the military police was such that -- if I'm not mistaken, they stated that only such people could be admitted who were devoted to the Croatian policy and implementation of the JCE. However, evidence shows otherwise. Document P2970 confirms that on the 26th of June, 1993, 25 to 30 per cent of the personnel of the 2nd Military Police Battalion was the percentage ascribed to the members of Muslim ethnicity. There is evidence in terms of exhibits and testimony who confirmed that throughout the period relevant to the indictment, the composition of the military police was multi-ethnic and that the commanders of individual units were Muslim. The Prosecution also referred to certain documents in their presentation which had nothing to do with Mr. Coric or the military police or with whatever they were talking about. One of such documents is P1088 pertaining to the construction of a thermal plant in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Another document is an order, P01087, which is neither Coric's command nor a command by the administration of the military police, and he wasn't on the list of addressees. Much like the situation was with these documents, we also heard certain references to the documents by the OTP which had nothing to do with Mr. Coric or they may have simply misinterpreted them. My learned friend Mr. Stringer, for example, at page 182 of the transcript, said that Mr. Coric, after the ultimatum, sent military police units to Gornji Vakuf to carry out ethnic cleansing. And today when my learned friend from the Prosecution spoke, he also said that in document P1053, I apologise if I'm mistaken about the number, he stated that Mr. Coric admitted to commanding the military police. The document I discussed was the interim report of Mr. Coric dated the 1st of January, 1993, which is before the ultimatum. There we can see that the military police were sent to the area to preserve peace and order, to protect the households and settlements as well as to establish regular traffic. There's no mention of any combat operations or ethnic cleansing. One of our colleagues from the Prosecution who spoke at transcript page 186, when referring to document 4177, P4177, said that it is a military police report sent to Coric, and they kept referring to it to show that Coric was allegedly made aware of the crimes happening in Prozor area. This report was not drafted by the military police. It wasn't sent to Valentin Coric. And when presenting it, the Prosecutor implied that, based on the events in Prozor, Coric could foresee what would follow in Mostar. However, this date -- document bears the date of the 14th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry. Apologies to interrupt. It's just that I don't want the Defence to be deprived of an opportunity to address the record and there's probably a mistake either way. P10188 was accurately reflected on the transcript, and appears to have been understood by my learned friend as P1088, but that's not reflected on the record. And then P10187, which I meant to say, has come out as P1087. So I think that's the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's at transcript page 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Is it clear enough for you, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, even if it was clear, I have no time to go back. So I will, with your permission, leave it to your personnel to check that. As regards events in Prozor, Defence has no time to respond in entirety to everything that was said by the Prosecutor. However, we discussed it in our appeal brief, in paragraphs 220, 221, 222, 223, as well as 224, and 225, and 226. There are many exhibits referred to in the footnotes referring to those paragraphs showing that the military police in Prozor was beyond Coric's control and the control of the military police administration. To continue, Your Honours, at some point, the Prosecutor said that Mr. Boban issued an order to Mr. Coric to deal with the situation in prisons. They referred to a handwritten remark on a specific document. We have no confirmation of either Mr. Coric receiving it or that it was ever acted upon. We wanted to draw your attention to our appeal paragraphs 141, 140, and to documents P5104, P5188, 3D915, P5199, 1D1704, and P7096. These documents clearly show who Mr. Boban sent the order to and who implemented it, and it was not Mr. Coric. As regards forcible labour carried out by the prisoners, the Prosecutor referred twice today to document P4039, asserting that the contents of the documents were seen through; i.e., that approval to take prisoners for labour should be obtained through the -- or from the administration of the military police. Your Honours, we saw in the trial thousands upon thousands of documents pertaining to people being taken for labour, and out of those thousands, one was located. However, there's no link to Mr. Coric or the police administration even in that single document, nor is there any evidence that such an order was issued. Could we please briefly move into private session? Because I will refer to a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents referred to by the Prosecution are P20235, P04424, and P02546. Those are the documents referred to by the Prosecution that relate to what I said in private session. I spoke earlier about Prozor, but I will now add just briefly. We had here in the courtroom Witness Zdenko Andabak, called by our Defence -- called by our Defence and believed to be not credible by the Prosecution. He cites the example of a promotion. It's true that Mr. Andabak was promoted but he didn't end up his career in the HVO. He ended up -- he ended his career in the military hierarchy of Bosnia-Herzegovina army. It is hard to believe that Mr. Andabak would have become a colonel of the BH army if he had been suspected in any way or if the authorities had believed him unfit for that position. The Prosecutor also mentioned that the military police dealt only with minor offences in Mostar. It didn't deal with serious crime. They dealt with cases of -- with failure to pay tax and similar which is simply not true. We have in registers 264 criminal reports made in cases involving Muslims as the injured party. Further, from document 5D043 -- 4236, we see that a criminal report was filed against a member of the HVO for murder of two persons, including one Muslim; then a criminal report against a number of HVO members also for murders of Muslims; then again -- just a moment. The next criminal report, I'll enumerate several more documents: 5D2095, 5D2097, P6727, 5D4169, 5D4168, 5D4154, 5D4165, 5D4231, P3571, P3483, P3523, P3508, P3513, P3482, P3497, 5D4183, 5D4240, 5D4242, 5D4243, 5D4248, 5D4249, 5D4255, 5D4212, 5D4194, P9465, 5D4199, P3118, 5D4207, P4139, 5D4201, 5D4203, 5D4200. Your Honours, we've heard also a Defence witness, member of the Criminal Investigations Department of the HVO, and his testimony goes precisely to filing of criminal reports against various members of the HVO for different offences and crimes against Muslims. Earlier today the Prosecutor invoked a report containing one sentence that says that for the time being, crimes committed by the Vinko Skrobo unit members and other units should only be recorded in such a way that they should be put in a very long drawer and forgotten. This is not true, Your Honours. They were recorded in preparation for a comprehensive operation that could not actually take place while civilian and military police were engaged at the front line instead of doing their regular work. This involved very well-armed groups for whose arrest and prosecution a very good plan was needed, if it was to stand any chance of success. This resulted eventually in an operation popularly known as Spider, Pauk, where these offenders were arrested and prosecuted. Witness Vidovic spoke about this on pages 41477 to 51481, and 51495 to 51499, 51500 to 51503. Also Witness Bandic on page 38214 to 38216, 38212 to 38213, and also document 3D422. Several times during his arguments the Prosecutor said that the Defence failed to cover this or did not pay attention to that. The Defence did, Your Honours, everything in its powers in the time allowed us. We have always been very clear and we stand by the same position we held from the very first day we entered this courtroom. We stand by everything we've said during the whole trial and in the appeal brief and in the reply and response, including my colleague's presentation and mine today in the courtroom. And I want to reiterate, we continue to affirm that the errors made during trial are such that they cannot be overlooked, that the judgement cannot stand, and that Mr. Coric has to be acquitted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. That brings us to the end of today's -- yes, Mr. Ivetic.
